manuscript_title: On the sensitivity of machine-learned probabilistic weather forecast

required_revisions.text: Resolve the anchor confound in Section 3.1. Either (a) rerun the comparison with symmetric anchor treatment (e.g. add an fES + 0.1 fES configuration, or report fGESgraph without the anchor), or (b) if no rerun is feasible, state explicitly in the abstract, Section 3.1 and Section 4.1 that the graph-energy configuration carries a 0.1 fES anchor the global-energy configuration lacks, and that the tropical difference therefore cannot be attributed to graph localization. Option (b) must remove any causal attribution language from the abstract.

Quantify the forecast-skill claims. Report multi-seed runs (>=3 seeds) for the three Section 3.1 configurations where compute allows; where it does not, report bootstrap confidence intervals over the 84 initialization dates with explicit sample sizes on all Figure 2 panels. Replace 'broadly similar', 'somewhat better' and 'some degradation' with mean differences and intervals.

Define a scalar metric for spectral fidelity against ERA5 (e.g. integrated log-ratio error over specified wavenumber bands) and tabulate it for all twelve configurations, so that 'substantially improves small-scale variability' is a measured quantity rather than a visual impression. Scale the wording in the abstract and Section 4.2 to whatever the metric shows.

Add a data and code availability statement (HARD gap, methods audit): deposit the custom scoring-rule implementations and training configs in a public repository, give an Anemoi commit hash or tagged release, and state whether trained checkpoints are available. Add a competing-interests statement.

Close the reproducibility HARD gaps identified by the methods audit: (a) state the exact train/validation/test partition of the 1979-2020 ERA5 period and confirm explicitly that 2022 is held out; (b) report random seeds and stochastic-element handling; (c) give PyTorch, Triton and spherical-harmonic-library versions and the ERA5 access/version details; (d) give the numerical values of the ad hoc multi-scale and spectral weighting factors and the exact Gaussian kernel specifications (standard deviations, boundary handling) currently described only as 'approximately 100/200/400/800 km'.

Add the promised sensitivity check on hyperparameters: a +/-50% perturbation of the scale/variable weighting factors and of the 0.1 anchor weight for at least one representative multi-scale experiment, reporting the resulting change in the spectral-fidelity metric. Without this the title's promise of a 'sensitivity analysis' is not met.

Rewrite the captions of Figures 3-14 so each specifies whether the panel shows absolute spectra or forecast/ERA5 ratios, the lead time(s) shown, and which of the twelve configurations each line corresponds to, with names consistent with Table 2 and a shared legend.

State the Section 3.1 architecture explicitly (embedding dimension, processor layers, encoder/decoder connectivity as actually run) and confirm whether it is comparable to the Section 3.2 configuration; state any deviations from Lang et al. (2024) beyond the O96 resolution restriction.

Tighten the novelty boundary: add the promised sentence crediting Lang et al. (2025) for the K-scale decomposition at the start of the Multi-Scale Score section and in Section 3.2, and state explicitly which spectral scores are introduced here for the first time. In the graph-score discussion, state plainly that no head-to-head patch-vs-graph comparison was run and that the contribution is structural (grid-agnostic, graph-native) rather than a demonstrated performance gain.

Revise the abstract: correct the grammatical errors, clarify the relationship between AIFS-CRPS and the trained variants, and rescale the 'viable alternative to CRPS-based training' framing to what single-run O96 experiments can support (e.g. 'competitive in our preliminary single-run comparison at O96').

minor_suggestions: Add the specific table or section reference in Pacchiardi et al. (2024) supporting the statement that patched energy scores 'performed best among multivariate scoring rules they considered', and make clear the comparison is among multivariate scores rather than against CRPS.

Note whether any source establishes propriety of the combined fGESgraph + 0.1 fES objective, or state explicitly that propriety of the combination is assumed from the propriety of each term and is not separately proved here.
State the ensemble size used in Section 3.2 and how ensemble members are initialized (perturbation scheme), which the methods audit flagged as unstated.
Report hardware type and approximate compute hours per configuration; this is a soft gap but helps readers judge the feasibility of the requested multi-seed runs.
State the forecast lead times evaluated in the Section 4.1 skill comparison, which are currently specified only for the spectral analysis.
Name the spherical-harmonic transform library used for the T191 truncation.

weaknesses.text: The abstract is difficult to parse and contains multiple grammatical errors that obscure the main contribution. Sentences like 'This note summarises preliminary study comparing versions of AIFS-CRPS, global weather forecast model, trained with different univariate and multivariate scoring rules aim to explicitly represent scale awareness' lack clear subject-verb agreement and are ambiguous about what is being compared.

Figures 3–14 are referenced collectively but their captions are minimal and repetitive ('Accumulated tendency spectra for geopotential at 500 hPa' appears four times with no distinction between panels). It is unclear from the captions alone what the difference is between Figures 3 and 4, or between 5 and 6, or how to interpret the ratio plots versus absolute spectra plots.

The paper does not explicitly state upfront which experiments use which loss configurations before diving into results. Table 1 and Table 2 appear late; the reader must infer from context which experiment corresponds to which result in Section 4.

In Section 3.2, the statement 'We used similar approach for spectral losses with per-waveband weighting. These weighting factors ad hoc and chosen only to of right order of magnitude' contains a grammatical error ('ad hoc and chosen only to of') and is vague about what 'right order of magnitude' means quantitatively.

The claim in Section 4.2 that 'edge-CRPS experiment and spectral magnitude CRPS experiment seem to slightly more successful' uses vague qualifier 'slightly' without quantification. How much is 'slightly'? Readers cannot determine the magnitude of difference from the text alone.

Figure references are inconsistent: the text refers to 'figure 2' (lowercase) in some places and 'Figure 2' (capitalized) in others, and the narrative flow between results and figures is unclear—e.g., 'see figure 2' appears mid-paragraph without clear indication of what aspect of the figure supports which claim.

The multi-scale loss formulation (Section 2, equations for L_K-scale) is presented abstractly without concrete specification of how the smoothing operators D_i are implemented in the experiments until Section 3.2, where it states 'four graph-based Gaussian smoothing operators on native O96 grid, with kernel widths of approximately 100, 200, 400, and 800 km.' The word 'approximately' introduces ambiguity about whether these are exact or estimated values.

The paper does not clearly state whether all 12 experiments in Section 3.2 use the same architecture and training data as Section 3.1, or whether the 'smaller model' and 'shorter training schedule' mentioned imply different hyperparameters. This is critical for interpreting whether differences are due to loss function or model capacity.

In Section 4.1, the statement 'conclusions also consistent when fair energy score or fair graph energy score used for verification instead of fair CRPS' is vague—it does not specify which conclusions or provide any numbers to support the claim that results are 'consistent.'

questions: Can the authors clarify the abstract? Specifically, what does 'versions of AIFS-CRPS, global weather forecast model' mean—are AIFS-CRPS and the global weather forecast model the same thing, or different? The sentence structure suggests ambiguity.

Figures 3–14: Can the captions be expanded to distinguish between absolute spectra plots and ratio plots, and to explain what the reader should look for in each? Currently, four figures have nearly identical captions.
In Section 3.2, what are the exact (not approximate) kernel widths used for the four Gaussian smoothing operators? If they are approximate, what is the tolerance?

Table 2 lists 12 experiments, but the text in Section 4.2 discusses results from these experiments without always making clear which experiment produced which result. Can the authors add a mapping between experiment names in Table 2 and the results discussed in Section 4.2?

In Section 4.1, when the authors state that 'conclusions also consistent when fair energy score or fair graph energy score used for verification,' can they provide specific numbers or figures showing this consistency?

Section 3.2 states the model uses 'embedding dimension of 256 and 12 processor layers' versus the unspecified architecture in Section 3.1. Can the authors clarify the architecture differences between the two experiment sets and confirm whether this affects the comparability of results?

The paper claims 'scale awareness alone does not guarantee realistic variability at all scales' (Section 4.2), but does not quantify what 'realistic' means. Is this assessed against ERA5 variance, or against some other metric?

In Section 2, the paper states that graph energy score 'may fail to strictly proper' and proposes combining it with a global anchor. Can the authors clarify whether the combined score (fGESgraph + 0.1 fES) is strictly proper, and if so, under what conditions?

weaknesses.text: No formal statistical test or confidence interval is provided for the main claim in Section 4.1 that 'forecast skill broadly similar across experiments'. The statement 'In extratropics, we do not find noticeable difference' is qualitative and unsupported by a hypothesis test, effect size, or CI. What threshold defines 'noticeable'?

Figure 2 shows CRPS values across regions but provides no error bars, confidence intervals, or sample sizes. The figure caption does not state how many forecast initializations or lead times are included in each panel, making it impossible to assess whether visual differences are within sampling noise.

Section 4.2 states 'Spectra computed from 2022 forecasts initialized every four days from 1 January to 1 December at 00 UTC, 84 initialization dates in total.' This is the only sample-size statement in the results, and it applies only to the spectral analysis. No n is given for the skill comparison in Section 4.1.

The claim that 'scale-aware losses improve spectral fidelity' (Discussion) is not quantified. No metric is defined for 'improvement', no statistical test compares spectral shapes across loss configurations, and no correction for multiple comparisons is applied across the twelve experiments in Table 2.

Figures 3–14 show spectral ratios (forecast/ERA5) but no confidence bands, bootstrap intervals, or uncertainty estimates. With only 84 initialization dates, sampling variability in spectral estimates could be substantial, especially at high wavenumbers, but this is not addressed.

The paper states 'weighting of different fields, scales, and variables can matter as much as, or more than, specific mechanism used to inject spatial awareness into loss' but provides no quantitative support (e.g., variance decomposition, effect sizes) for this claim.

No multiple-comparison correction is applied or discussed despite twelve loss configurations being tested in Section 3.2. If visual differences in spectral plots are being used to rank loss configurations, the family-wise error rate or false discovery rate should be controlled.

The 'ad hoc' weighting factors for small scales (mentioned in Section 3.2: 'These weighting factors ad hoc and chosen only to of right order of magnitude - estimated from data - rather than tuned') introduce an unquantified source of bias. How sensitive are the spectral results to these choices?

No ablation study or sensitivity analysis is provided to isolate the contribution of different components (e.g., graph connectivity, smoothing kernel widths, spectral truncation) to the observed differences in spectra.

questions: In Section 4.1, what is the sample size (number of forecast initializations, lead times, or grid points) underlying each CRPS value in Figure 2? How are error bars or confidence intervals computed, and why are they not shown?

For the claim that 'graph energy score experiment appears to perform best' in the tropics (Section 4.1), what is the magnitude of the difference in CRPS between graph energy and CRPS, and is it statistically significant? Please provide a test statistic, p-value, and 95% CI for the difference.

In Section 4.2, were the twelve loss configurations pre-specified before observing the spectral results, or were they selected post-hoc based on preliminary findings? If post-hoc, a multiple-comparison correction (e.g., Bonferroni or FDR) should be applied to any claims about which configurations perform best.

How were the 'ad hoc' weighting factors for small scales (Section 3.2) chosen? Please provide the estimated values and a sensitivity analysis showing how spectral results change if these weights are perturbed by ±50%.

Figures 3–14 show spectral ratios but no confidence intervals or uncertainty bands. With n=84 initializations, what is the approximate 95% CI width for spectral estimates at high wavenumbers (e.g., ℓ=180)? Do the visual differences between loss configurations exceed this uncertainty?

The paper claims 'making forecast scores scale-aware substantially improves small-scale variability' (Section 4.2). Please quantify 'substantially' with an effect size (e.g., percent change in spectral power at small scales) and a statistical test comparing scale-aware vs. scale-unaware losses.

In Section 3.1, were the three experiments (CRPS, global energy, graph energy) the only ones planned, or were other loss configurations tested and not reported? If the latter, please disclose the full set of experiments conducted to avoid selective reporting.

weaknesses.text: No explicit statement of competing interests or conflicts of interest, even a simple 'none declared' statement would strengthen transparency.

No data or code availability statement provided, despite the use of public data and open-source framework; authors should clarify whether trained model weights, experimental configurations, and analysis scripts are or will be made available.

questions: Will the trained model weights, hyperparameter configurations, and analysis scripts be made available in a repository (e.g., GitHub, Zenodo) to enable reproducibility and reuse?

Do the authors have any competing interests, financial or otherwise, related to this work or the institutions/funding bodies involved? An explicit statement (even 'none') would be appropriate for a public review.
Are there any restrictions on use of the ERA5 data or Anemoi framework that should be disclosed to readers?

weaknesses.text: Patched energy score claim not verified: The manuscript states (Section 1, Introduction) that "In weather forecasting experiments of [19], patched energy scores performed best among multivariate scoring rules they considered." This is presented as motivation for the graph-based approach, but the manuscript does not cite specific results or figures from [19] to support this claim. The reader cannot verify whether [19] actually concluded this or whether the claim is accurately characterized.

Sparse related-work section: The Introduction and Discussion do not systematically review competing approaches to scale-aware training in machine-learned weather forecasting. The manuscript mentions that "different ways have proposed to improve spectral representation" and lists several approaches, but does not critically compare these approaches or explain why the present study's approach is distinct or complementary.

Missing discussion of strict propriety of graph energy score: The manuscript acknowledges (Section 2, Graph Energy Score) that "graph energy score, however, may fail to strictly proper" and notes that strict propriety may be recovered under additional assumptions, but then cites [19] as justification for combining it with a global anchor without discussing whether the combined score (fGESgraph + 0.1 fES) is strictly proper or citing a source that establishes this.

No citation for verification of "almost fair CRPS" concept: The manuscript introduces the "almost fair CRPS" (afCRPS) as a convex combination of fair and standard CRPS, citing [13] as the source, but does not verify whether [13] actually introduced this variant or merely used it.

Limited discussion of why multivariate scores should improve tropical forecasts: The manuscript observes (Section 4.1) that "in tropics, graph energy score experiment appears to perform best, while energy score experiment shows some degradation," but there is no discussion of why multivariate scores might be expected to perform differently in the tropics versus extratropics, or citation of prior work on this regional dependence.

questions: In Section 1, you state that patched energy scores "performed best among multivariate scoring rules" in [19]. Can you cite the specific figure, table, or result from [19] that supports this claim?
For the combined loss L_graph = fGESgraph + 0.1 fES used in Section 3.1, is the combined score strictly proper? If so, is this established in [19] or elsewhere, or is it an assumption you are making?

The manuscript notes that graph energy score "may fail to strictly proper" but then uses it in training. What is the practical implication of this for the forecast skill results in Section 4.1? Does the weak global anchor sufficiently recover propriety for your purposes?

In Section 4.1, you observe regional differences (extratropics vs. tropics) in the sensitivity to scoring rules. Is there prior work on why multivariate spatial scores might be more or less effective in different climate regimes, or is this an open question you are flagging?

The manuscript mentions that "weighting of different fields, scales, and variables can matter as much as, or more than, the specific mechanism used to inject spatial awareness into loss" (Discussion). Are there prior studies on the sensitivity of machine-learned weather models to these weighting choices, or is this a novel observation from your experiments?

weaknesses.text: HARD: Section 3.1 compares three loss functions (CRPS, global energy score, graph energy score) but does not isolate the source of differences. The graph energy score experiment includes a weak global energy score anchor (L_graph = fGESgraph + 0.1 fES), while the global energy score experiment uses only fES. This confounds the effect of localization (graph vs. global) with the effect of the anchor term. To isolate localization, the design should compare fGESgraph + 0.1 fES (graph with anchor) against fES + 0.1 fES (global with anchor) or fGESgraph alone (graph without anchor). As written, the superiority of graph energy in the tropics (Figure 2) cannot be attributed to the graph structure itself.

HARD: Section 3.2 tests twelve loss configurations (Table 2) but lacks a systematic factorial design to decompose the effects of (i) multivariate vs. univariate scoring, (ii) localization strategy (global, graph, edge), (iii) scale decomposition (single-scale vs. multi-scale), and (iv) weighting (unweighted vs. per-scale/per-variable weighting). The authors state 'weighting of different fields, scales, and variables can matter as much as, or more than, specific mechanism used to inject spatial awareness' (Section 5), but this conclusion rests on visual inspection of spectra (Figures 3–14) rather than a controlled comparison. For example, comparing 'Multi-scale CRPS' (Table 2) to 'Spectral magnitude CRPS weighted' conflates scale decomposition method, weighting scheme, and spectral representation. A factorial design with orthogonal variation would clarify which factors drive the observed differences.

HARD: The claim that 'scale-aware losses improve spectral fidelity' (Section 5) is based on visual comparison of spectral ratios in Figures 3–14, but no quantitative metric (e.g., RMS error in spectral amplitude, Kolmogorov-Smirnov test against ERA5 spectrum) is provided to support this claim. The figures show that different losses produce different spectra, but 'improvement' is not formally defined or measured. Which loss is 'better'—one that matches ERA5 at all scales, or one that slightly overcompensates at small scales (as noted in Section 4.2)? Without a metric, the comparison is subjective.

HARD: The experiments in Section 3.2 use a 'smaller model' and 'shorter training schedule' (Section 3.2) to reduce computational cost, but the manuscript does not specify the model size, training duration, or learning rates for these experiments. This prevents assessment of whether the spectral results are robust to the reduced training regime or whether they reflect incomplete convergence. The authors note that 'greater model capacity and longer training may improve performance of losses without scale awareness or reduce differences between experiments' (Section 5), but this is speculation without evidence.

HARD: The manuscript does not report confidence intervals, error bars, or statistical significance tests for the forecast skill comparisons in Figure 2 or the spectral comparisons in Figures 3–14. The results are presented as point estimates from a single training run per configuration (implied by 'we run three experiments' in Section 3.1 and the singular 'we use' in Section 3.2). Without replication, it is impossible to distinguish signal from noise, especially in the tropics where differences appear small (Figure 2, right panels).

HARD: The paper claims that 'graph energy score experiment performs best' in the tropics (Section 4.1, Figure 2), but the figure shows only modest visual differences between the three experiments, and no quantitative comparison (e.g., mean absolute error, correlation) is provided. The claim of superiority is not supported by a statistical test or a clear quantitative metric.

SOFT: The choice of hyperparameters for the multi-scale and spectral experiments (e.g., kernel widths of 100, 200, 400, 800 km; spectral truncation T191; waveband groupings) is described as 'ad hoc and chosen only to be of right order of magnitude—estimated from data—rather than tuned' (Section 3.2). This introduces an uncontrolled source of variation: different hyperparameter choices might favor different loss functions. A sensitivity analysis varying these parameters would strengthen the conclusions.

SOFT: The manuscript does not compare the proposed graph-based localization to the patch-based localization of Pacchiardi et al. (2024, ref. 19), which is cited as motivation. The authors state that graph-based localization is 'more flexible' but provide no empirical evidence that it outperforms patch-based approaches on the same task.

SOFT: The spectral analysis aggregates results over all 84 initialization dates in 2022 but does not stratify by weather regime (e.g., blocking, cyclones, trade winds) or season. Spectral properties may vary substantially across regimes, and a loss function that performs well on average may perform poorly in specific conditions. Regime-stratified analysis would provide more actionable insights.

The manuscript uses 'accumulated tendency spectra' (differences between forecast and initial state) as the diagnostic, but does not justify why this is the appropriate metric for assessing forecast realism. Accumulated tendencies reflect the model's ability to generate changes, but they may not directly correlate with forecast skill or physical plausibility of the forecast state itself.

questions: Section 3.1: Why does the graph energy score experiment include a weak global energy score anchor (L_graph = fGESgraph + 0.1 fES) while the global energy score experiment does not? To isolate the effect of localization, should both experiments include an anchor term?

Section 3.1: Figure 2 shows only modest differences between the three training objectives, especially in the extratropics. Are these differences statistically significant, or could they reflect noise from a single training run? Can the authors provide error bars or confidence intervals?

Section 3.2: How were the hyperparameters (kernel widths, spectral truncation, waveband groupings) chosen? Were they tuned on a validation set, or estimated from the training data? How sensitive are the spectral results to these choices?

Section 3.2: The authors state that 'weighting of different fields, scales, and variables can matter as much as, or more than, specific mechanism used to inject spatial awareness' (Section 5). Can you provide a controlled comparison isolating the effect of weighting from the effect of the scoring rule or scale decomposition method?

Section 4.2: What quantitative metric is used to assess whether a loss function 'improves' spectral fidelity? How is 'improvement' defined relative to ERA5? Are the differences in Figures 3–14 statistically significant?

Section 4.2: The manuscript notes that 'some experiments show slight overcompensation for some variables, where early lead-time tendencies contain less small-scale variability than ERA5 reference tendency.' Which experiments show this, and is overcompensation considered desirable or undesirable?

Section 3.2: What are the model size, embedding dimension, number of layers, and training duration for the experiments in Section 3.2? The text mentions 'embedding dimension of 256 and 12 processor layers' but does not specify the number of optimization steps or wall-clock training time.

Section 4.1: The claim that graph energy score 'performs somewhat better' in the tropics (Abstract, Section 4.1) is based on visual inspection of Figure 2. Can you quantify this difference (e.g., mean CRPS, correlation with observations) and test for statistical significance?

Section 4.2: Why are accumulated tendency spectra the appropriate diagnostic for forecast realism? How do they relate to forecast skill (e.g., CRPS, anomaly correlation) or physical plausibility of the forecast state?

Section 5: The authors acknowledge that 'greater model capacity and longer training may improve performance of losses without scale awareness or reduce differences between experiments.' Can you provide evidence (e.g., learning curves, convergence diagnostics) that the models in Section 3.2 have converged?

weaknesses.text: Multi-scale loss formulation is from Lang et al. (2025, arXiv:2506.10868), not a novel contribution of this work. The manuscript applies this existing formulation to new scoring rules but does not clearly state this boundary. Section 2.8 and experiments in Section 3.2 should explicitly credit Lang et al. (2025) as the source of the multi-scale approach.

Graph energy score is presented without clear novelty justification. The manuscript acknowledges it is 'similar to patched energy score' (Pacchiardi et al. 2024) but does not explain what is genuinely new beyond using k-nearest-neighbor graphs instead of rectangular patches. No experimental comparison to patch-based localization is provided.

Graph variogram score and graph edge energy score lack novelty statements. These are straightforward extensions of existing scores (variogram score from Scheuerer & Hamill 2015; energy score) to graph neighborhoods, but the manuscript does not explicitly state this or justify why these variants are worth introducing.

Spectral scoring rules are not established as novel. The manuscript introduces 'spectral energy score' and 'spectral magnitude CRPS' without citing prior work, then later mentions FourCastNet 3 uses 'spectral loss term like spectral magnitude CRPS,' suggesting this is not new. Novelty should be clarified.

Experimental results are confirmatory, not surprising. All objectives are proper scoring rules; the finding that 'forecast skill broadly similar' and 'differences between scale-aware loss objectives comparatively small' (Section 4.2) does not advance understanding of why one would prefer one score over another.

No head-to-head comparison to closest prior work. The manuscript cites Pacchiardi et al. (2024) on patched energy scores but does not experimentally compare graph-based vs. patch-based localization. Similarly, no direct comparison to Lang et al. (2025) results is provided.

Claimed generalizability of graph approach is not demonstrated. The paper states the graph method 'can in principle applied on irregular grids, sparse spatial meshes, or sparse observation networks' (Section 2) but provides no experiments on non-regular grids. This should be either demonstrated or removed.

Spectral weighting is ad hoc. The manuscript states weighting factors are 'ad hoc and chosen only to be of right order of magnitude—estimated from data—rather than tuned' (Section 3.2). No ablation studies test sensitivity to these choices, undermining confidence in the spectral results.

Limited model capacity and resolution. Experiments use O96 (~1°) resolution and 8-member ensembles. The authors acknowledge (Section 5) that 'greater model capacity and longer training may improve performance of losses without scale awareness or reduce differences between experiments,' which undermines generalizability of findings.

Missing ablations on design choices. The graph energy score uses k=16 nearest neighbors without ablation. Multi-scale experiments use four smoothing operators with specific kernel widths (100, 200, 400, 800 km) without justification.

questions: Is the multi-scale loss formulation (Section 2.8) entirely from Lang et al. (2025), or have you made modifications? If modifications exist, what are they and how do they constitute a novel contribution?
Have you experimentally compared graph-based localization to the patched energy scores of Pacchiardi et al. (2024)? If not, why not?
Are the spectral energy score and spectral magnitude CRPS formulations original to this work, or are they standard practice in the field? Please cite any prior use.

For graph variogram score and graph edge energy score: are these novel contributions, or straightforward extensions of existing scores to graph neighborhoods? Please clarify the novelty boundary explicitly.
How sensitive are the spectral results (Figures 3–14) to the ad hoc weighting choices? Can you provide ablation studies?
Can you demonstrate the claimed applicability of the graph approach to irregular grids, sparse meshes, or sparse observation networks, or should this be framed as future work?
Is the tropical improvement of graph energy score (Section 4.1) statistically significant? What is the magnitude of improvement in absolute terms?
How would results change with the full-resolution AIFS-CRPS model rather than the O96 reduced version? Is this planned?

weaknesses.text: No code repository is provided or referenced with a commit hash or DOI. The manuscript states 'All scores implemented in Anemoi framework' (Abstract) and later 'We use Anemoi framework (https://github.com/ecmwf/anemoi-core)' (Section 3.1), but provides no version, branch, or commit identifier, and does not state whether custom scoring-rule implementations are deposited anywhere.

No trained model weights, checkpoints, or intermediate outputs are deposited or promised with an accession number. The results in Section 4 depend entirely on these models, which cannot be inspected or reused without them.

Random seeds are not specified for any experiment. The manuscript uses AdamW optimizer and neural network training but does not state whether results are averaged over multiple runs, what seeds were used, or whether seed-averaging was performed.

Software versions are missing for critical dependencies: PyTorch (referenced via torch.compile, Section 3.1), Triton (Section 3.1), the spherical harmonic transform library (Section 3.2: 'spherical harmonic transform with truncation T191'), and the ERA5 data loader. These affect numerical reproducibility.

Hyperparameter choices in Section 3.2 are explicitly described as ad hoc: 'These weighting factors ad hoc and chosen only to be of right order of magnitude - estimated from data - rather than tuned.' No ablation study, sensitivity analysis, or justification is provided for the scale weights ζ_i, spectral band boundaries (0–10, 11–20, 21–80, 81–120, 121–191), or Gaussian smoothing kernel widths (100, 200, 400, 800 km). Without this, the spectral results (Figures 3–14) cannot be independently validated or understood to be robust.

Data preprocessing is not fully specified. The manuscript states 'Training uses ERA5 reanalysis data from 1979 to 2020, and inference performed for 2022' (Section 3.1) but does not describe: normalization/standardization procedures, handling of missing values, interpolation to the O96 grid, or train/validation/test split logic. These are load-bearing for reproducibility.

The encoder–processor–decoder architecture is described as following 'AIFS-CRPS [13]' but Section 3.1 states 'we restrict resolution here to O96 ≈ 1 deg model' without specifying embedding dimension, number of processor layers, or other hyperparameters for the Section 3.1 experiments. Section 3.2 specifies 'embedding dimension of 256 and 12 processor layers' but only for the cheaper configuration, not the main experiments.

The graph connectivity for graph-based scores is defined as 'k-nearest-neighbour graph with k=16 on O96 reduced Gaussian grid' (Section 3.1) but the method for computing nearest neighbours (Euclidean? geodesic? on the sphere?) and tie-breaking are not specified.

Spectral analysis methodology (Section 4.2) lacks detail: How are spectra computed from ensemble forecasts (per-member or ensemble-mean)? The text states 'we average spectra over all ensemble members' but does not clarify whether this is done before or after taking the ratio to ERA5. How are the 84 initialization dates (Section 4.2) combined into a single spectrum (mean? median?)? What is the confidence interval or uncertainty estimate?

Figures 3–14 are difficult to interpret without a legend or caption explaining which line/color corresponds to which experiment. The captions repeat the same text ('Accumulated tendency spectra for [variable] at 500 hPa') without distinguishing between Figures 3 and 4, or between spectra and ratios. This appears to be a formatting error that obscures the results.

The paper states 'we compute spectra of accumulated forecast tendencies' (Section 4.2) but does not define how accumulated tendencies are computed from multi-step forecasts. Are they computed at each lead time separately and then averaged? Are they computed as the difference between the final forecast and the initial state?

No statement is made about whether code or data will be deposited upon publication, or under what conditions they will be made available. The acknowledgments mention the Anemoi framework but do not commit to releasing the experimental code or models.

The training schedule differs between Section 3.1 (150k steps at rollout 1, 30k at rollout 2, 1k per step from 3–12) and Section 3.2 (150k steps one-step, then 1k per step up to 8). It is unclear whether these are the only two configurations tested or whether other schedules were explored and not reported.

questions: What is the exact version (commit hash or release tag) of the Anemoi framework used for these experiments, and where are the custom scoring-rule implementations deposited?
Are trained model weights, optimizer states, or checkpoints available for download or inspection? If not, will they be deposited upon publication, and under what accession?
What random seeds were used for model initialization, data shuffling, and any stochastic components of training? Were results averaged over multiple runs, and if so, how many?
What are the exact versions of PyTorch, Triton, and the spherical harmonic transform library (e.g., SHTns, pyshtools) used? Do results depend on specific hardware (GPU model, CUDA version)?

How were the ad hoc weighting factors (scale weights ζ_i, spectral band boundaries, Gaussian kernel widths) chosen? Can you provide an ablation study or sensitivity analysis showing how results change if these are varied?

Can you provide a step-by-step description of data preprocessing: normalization, handling of missing values, interpolation to O96, train/validation/test split, and any other transformations applied to ERA5 data before training?
For Section 3.1 experiments, what are the embedding dimension and number of processor layers? Are these the same as in Section 3.2 (256 and 12)?
How are nearest neighbours computed for the k-nearest-neighbour graph (Euclidean distance on the grid, geodesic distance on the sphere, or something else)? How are ties broken?
In Section 4.2, how are spectra aggregated across the 84 initialization dates? Are they averaged, and if so, is a confidence interval or standard error provided?
Figures 3–14 appear to have duplicate or unclear captions. Can you clarify which figures show spectra vs. ratios, and provide a legend identifying each experiment?
Will code and trained models be made available upon publication? If so, under what license and with what accession number or repository URL?

weaknesses.text: The abstract claims 'multivariate scores [are] viable alternative to CRPS-based training for global machine-learned weather forecasting' but the evidence is limited to one low-resolution experiment (O96) with a small model and short training schedule. The phrase 'viable alternative' implies broad applicability not demonstrated here. This is a HARD overclaim: the results show multivariate scores perform comparably in extratropics and slightly better in tropics at one resolution, not that they are a proven alternative for operational forecasting.

The title 'On the sensitivity of machine-learned probabilistic weather forecast models to scale-aware scoring rules' promises a sensitivity analysis but the paper does not quantify sensitivity (e.g., no error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical tests on the differences shown in Figure 2). The visual differences in Figure 2 are described qualitatively ('small differences', 'somewhat better', 'some degradation') without statistical support. This is HARD: a sensitivity analysis requires quantified measures of how much the output changes with input variation.

The abstract states 'forecast skill broadly similar' across methods but provides no statistical test or effect-size estimate to support this claim. Figure 2 shows spatial maps but no summary statistics, p-values, or confidence intervals. The claim 'broadly similar' is defensible visually but unsupported quantitatively. This is SOFT: the claim is hedged ('broadly') but lacks the rigor expected for a primary result.

Section 4.2 (spectra analysis) is largely descriptive. The paper shows that scale-aware losses improve small-scale variability (Figures 3–14) but does not quantify the magnitude of improvement or test whether differences are statistically significant. The statement 'making forecast scores scale-aware substantially improves small-scale variability' (Discussion) is not backed by a metric or test. This is SOFT: the conclusion is reasonable from the figures but overstated without quantification.

The paper states 'differences between scale-aware loss objectives comparatively small' (Section 4.2) but does not define 'small' or provide a metric. This is SOFT: the claim is vague and would benefit from a quantitative threshold or comparison to a baseline.

The claim that 'weighting of different fields, scales, and variables can matter as much as, or more than, specific mechanism used to inject spatial awareness' (Discussion) is based on visual inspection of Figures 3–14 and is not quantified. No ablation study or statistical test isolates the contribution of weighting vs. mechanism. This is SOFT: the observation is plausible but presented as a conclusion without evidence.

The paper does not report how many initialization dates or forecast lead times were used to compute the spectra in Section 4.2. It states '84 initialization dates in total' but does not specify the lead time range over which spectra were averaged. This affects the interpretability of the results. This is SOFT: procedural clarity is needed.

The abstract claims the study 'analyse[s] how different scoring rules and scale-aware loss constraints shape spectra of forecast fields' but the analysis is observational (showing spectra) rather than mechanistic (explaining why). The paper does not isolate which component of the loss (e.g., multivariate structure vs. scale weighting) drives the spectral changes. This is SOFT: the framing overstates the depth of analysis.

The paper uses ad hoc weighting factors for multi-scale experiments ('chosen only to be of right order of magnitude - estimated from data - rather than tuned', Section 3.2). This introduces an uncontrolled variable that could confound comparisons. The authors acknowledge this but do not test sensitivity to these choices. This is SOFT: a sensitivity analysis on weighting factors would strengthen the claims.

questions: Figure 2 shows spatial maps but no global summary statistics. What are the mean CRPS differences (and confidence intervals or standard errors) between the three experiments across the full domain and at each lead time? Without this, the claim 'forecast skill broadly similar' cannot be verified.

In Section 4.2, over what lead-time range were the accumulated tendency spectra computed? The paper states spectra were computed from 'forecasts initialized every four days' but does not specify whether all lead times (1–8 steps) were pooled or analyzed separately. This affects interpretation.

How were the ad hoc weighting factors in Section 3.2 chosen? The paper states they were 'estimated from data' but does not specify the procedure. Were they tuned on the training set, validation set, or test set? A sensitivity analysis varying these factors by ±50% would clarify their impact.

The paper claims graph energy score 'performs somewhat better' in the tropics (Abstract) but Figure 2 (right column) shows only visual differences. What is the magnitude of the difference in CRPS or another metric, and is it statistically significant at the 95% confidence level?

In Section 2, the paper states that graph energy score 'may fail to be strictly proper' but then combines it with a weak global anchor to recover propriety. How sensitive are the results to the weight of this anchor (0.1 in the experiments)? Was this weight tuned or chosen a priori?

The paper compares twelve loss configurations in Section 3.2 but uses a smaller model and shorter training schedule than Section 3.1 to 'reduce computational cost'. How do the results in Section 3.1 (full model) compare to the corresponding experiments in Section 3.2 (reduced model)? Without this, it is unclear whether the spectral conclusions generalize.

The Discussion states 'greater model capacity and longer training may improve performance of losses without scale awareness or reduce differences between experiments'. This is a major caveat. What is the minimum model capacity or training duration needed to draw robust conclusions? Can the authors provide a brief experiment at intermediate scale to bound this uncertainty?
